JUSTIN - START HERE
===================

*******************************************************************************
UPDATE 2026-08-09 14:20 -- THIS ALL WORKS NOW. RAN ON THE BOARD.

  256 tokens generated on the FPGA, output byte-identical to expected_output.txt.
  Measured 1.020 s/token (0.98 tok/s).

Two things the steps below do not tell you, both discovered the hard way:

  1. THE SYSTEM IS DUAL-CORE. Two Nios II, two JTAG UARTs, and no .jdi file to
     tell them apart, so the tools refuse to connect at all until you say which:

         nios2-terminal --device 1 --instance 0
         nios2-download -c "USB-Blaster [USB-0]" --device 1 --instance 0 -g llama.elf

     Without --instance you get "There are two or more Nios II CPUs...".

  2. STALE OUTPUT LOOKS LIKE A BUG. A previous program keeps running after you
     close the terminal, and its buffered bytes show up in your NEXT session --
     the middle of an old story spliced onto a new one. Reset and drain first:

         nios2-download ... -r llama.elf     # halt the old one
         (open a throwaway nios2-terminal for 5s, close it)

Good news: the linker-region trap does NOT fire on this system. nios2-bsp maps
everything to SDRAM by itself. Verified by section address, not by dialog.

Full measurements and the reason it is 1 s/token and not 0.1:
docs/HARDWARE-RESULTS.md
*******************************************************************************

Everything you need is in this folder -- no downloads, no .bin files, nothing to
pip install. Run the steps in order. Anything you can do before Quartus 18.1
finishes installing is marked NOW.

If you are reading this from a git clone, you already have everything:

    git clone https://github.com/wilsonwu-ai/vibe-silicon
    cd vibe-silicon/dist/llama-nios

Files here:

    run_baremetal.c      the program
    model260k.h          the weights, as a C array (5.5 MB of text, 1,056,540
                         bytes of model). There is no filesystem on the board,
                         so the model is compiled into the executable.
    tok512.h             the tokenizer, same deal
    expected_output.txt  exactly what it should print, seed 42
    bridge.py            forwards board output to the public page
    README.txt           the same build info, without the hand-holding

Still installing? Quartus Prime Lite 18.1 + Intel FPGA Monitor Program 18.1,
NOT 24.1 or newer -- Nios II was removed. Download links, the exact .qdz you
need, and the "tick the Nios II EDS component" warning are in board/README.md
in the repo. 18.1 coexists with your 25.1; you do not have to uninstall.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 1  (NOW - needs nothing but the Quartus 25.1 you already have)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Prove the board is alive. This does NOT need Nios II, and the Programmer works
in every Quartus version.

    jtagconfig

You want to see a USB-Blaster with a 10M50 device.

  - "not recognised"?  jtagconfig is not on PATH. Run it from the Quartus
    command prompt, or call it by full path out of <quartus>\quartus\bin64.
  - Nothing listed?    It is the driver. It lives under <quartus>\drivers --
                       point Device Manager at that folder for the unrecognised
                       USB device.
  - Still nothing?     Different cable, different USB port. The board is
                       confirmed working (it arrived running the factory
                       7-segment demo).

If you also want to prove the Programmer path end to end, load any .sof onto
the board and watch the LEDs change. Any .sof will do -- the DE10-Lite System CD
from terasic.com has several, or just wait for Step 3, where the Monitor Program
supplies one. Do not burn time hunting for the CD; jtagconfig seeing the 10M50
is the answer that actually matters.

Do this while 18.1 installs. Finding a driver problem now instead of at 3pm is
worth an hour.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 2  (NOW - no board needed, no Nios II needed)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Prove the public page works from your machine. Ask Wilson for the token.

    python bridge.py --token <TOKEN> --replay expected_output.txt --cps 12

Open https://vibe-silicon.wilson-af8.workers.dev and you should see words
appearing. The page will label it "streaming - recorded run", because it is.

If that works, the whole network path from your PC to the public demo is proven
before the board is even in the picture.

Needs only the Python standard library. Nothing to pip install. If "python"
opens the Microsoft Store, use "py" instead.

WHEN IT WORKS, CLEAR IT:

    python bridge.py --token <TOKEN> --reset

Otherwise that recorded text sits in the page's buffer, and anyone loading the
page later sees a recording that we would rather not have to explain.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 3  (after Quartus 18.1 + Intel FPGA Monitor Program 18.1 are installed)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

WHY THE MONITOR PROGRAM AT ALL, IF JTAG SERIAL ALREADY WORKS

It is not an IDE you have to adopt. Everything is drivable from the command
line, and you have already proven those tools work.

What you need from it is ONE artifact: a prebuilt CPU. This board has no
processor, so something has to put a Nios II core + SDRAM controller + JTAG
UART into the fabric. Building that yourself in Platform Designer is hours of
Qsys and SDRAM timing closure. The Monitor Program ships it ready-made as the
"DE10-Lite Computer".

Open it once to get that onto the board and to get the linker settings. Then
ignore the GUI and work from the shell.

Get **18.1**, not 21.1 -- FPGA Academy's own instruction is to match your
Quartus version.

ALTERNATIVE, if the Monitor Program fights you: the Terasic DE10-Lite System CD
ships "SDRAM Test in Nios II", which is also a real Nios II + SDRAM + JTAG UART
design for this board. It works, but it is a memory test and probably has no
hardware FPU -- and our model is floating point throughout, so that is the
difference between ~0.1 s and ~3 s per word.

WORTH RUNNING EITHER WAY: the Terasic SDRAM test proves the 64 MB physically
works before we put a 1.8 MB program into it. If ours later hangs, that tells
you whether to suspect the memory or the linker regions.


Confirm the toolchain exists -- Start Menu > Nios II Command Shell, then:

    nios2-elf-gcc --version

Then, in the Monitor Program:

    File > New Project
      > select the "DE10-Lite Computer" predesigned system
      > load one of the BUNDLED SAMPLE C PROGRAMS
      > Compile, Load, Run

Do the stock sample FIRST, before ours. If it prints to the terminal window, the
prebuilt bitstream, the JTAG UART and the compiler are all working, and anything
that breaks after this point is our code, not the setup.

While you are here, WRITE DOWN THE PATH to the DE10-Lite Computer's .sof. The
Monitor Program installs it under its Computer_Systems folder and programs it
for you when it loads a project. You need it by hand in Step 5, and you need it
again after every power cycle -- MAX 10 reloads its factory image from on-chip
flash when it loses power, and the Nios II core simply is not there any more.

    .sof path: ______________________________________________

>>> THE ONE SETTING THAT SILENTLY EATS AN HOUR <<<

In the BSP / Monitor Program linker settings, put .text .rodata .data .bss heap
and stack in SDRAM (0x00000000, 64 MB). NOT the 64 KB on-chip RAM.

Our program needs about 1.8 MB, and the model is const, so it lands in .rodata
-- that section alone is 1 MB. It does not fit on-chip, and the failure mode is
a HANG WITH NO ERROR MESSAGE. If nothing prints later, check this first.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 4  (build ours)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Same Monitor Program project flow as the sample you just ran. That is on purpose:
the Monitor Program owns the BSP, the linker script and the stdio-to-JTAG-UART
wiring, and none of that comes for free from a bare gcc command line.

    File > New Project
      > "DE10-Lite Computer" again
      > program type: C Program
      > source file: run_baremetal.c   (from THIS folder)
      > linker settings: everything in SDRAM, as in Step 3
      > Compile

model260k.h and tok512.h must sit in the same folder as run_baremetal.c. They
already do -- just do not move the .c file out on its own.

Compiling takes a minute or two and looks stuck. It is not stuck: model260k.h is
5.5 MB of hex and gcc is chewing through it. Let it finish.

If you would rather drive it from the Nios II Command Shell, the compile itself
is one line, run from inside this folder:

    nios2-elf-gcc -O2 -mcustom-fpu-cfg=60-2 run_baremetal.c -o llama.elf -lm

  ... but that ELF has no system linker script, so it will not boot on the
  board. Use it only to check that the code compiles. To produce a runnable ELF
  on the command line you need the BSP's linker script and crt0 from a generated
  BSP, which is exactly what the Monitor Program is doing for you above.

  If -mcustom-fpu-cfg=60-2 errors, DROP IT. Soft float still works, just
  slower. That is a speed problem, not a correctness problem.

No objcopy, no .bin files, no symbol-name games. If you have seen an older
version of these instructions that had you run nios2-elf-objcopy on
stories260K.bin, ignore it -- see APPENDIX at the bottom for why.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 5  (run it)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Monitor Program: Load, then Run. It programs the .sof and downloads the ELF for
you, and its own terminal window shows the output.

By hand, from the Nios II Command Shell:

    quartus_pgm -m jtag -o "p;<path to DE10-Lite_Computer.sof>"
    nios2-download -c "USB-Blaster [USB-0]" -g llama.elf
    nios2-terminal

ONLY ONE PROGRAM CAN OWN THE USB-BLASTER AT A TIME. Close the Quartus Programmer
from Step 1, close any Monitor Program session, and close any other
nios2-terminal before running these. A busy cable produces confusing errors that
look like board failures and are not.

The ELF is about 1.1 MB, so expect 9-70 seconds to load over JTAG. Then words
start appearing one at a time.

It should say:

    Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play
    outside in the sun. One day, her mom asked her to teach him a nice way to
    play in the sun.

Full expected text is in expected_output.txt. The seed is fixed at 42, so this
is deterministic -- you should get exactly those words.

  - Right words      -> it works. Time 256 tokens with a stopwatch and send
                        Wilson the seconds-per-token. We want a measured number
                        on the slide, not an estimate.
  - Different words  -> tell Wilson, and say whether you built the Step 4 way or
                        the appendix way. Wrong-but-readable output is the
                        signature of a misaligned model blob, which only the
                        objcopy route can produce.
  - Garbage/nothing  -> linker regions. See Step 3.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
STEP 6  (put it on the public page)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ORDER MATTERS. The program prints its story once and exits. If the board has
already finished, the bridge attaches to a board with nothing left to say and
the page stays empty.

First shell -- start the bridge and leave it running:

    python bridge.py --token <TOKEN> --reset

It spawns nios2-terminal itself, so make sure the one from Step 5 is closed.
It mirrors everything in your console so you can watch too.

Second shell -- now re-run the program:

    nios2-download -c "USB-Blaster [USB-0]" -g llama.elf

Words appear in the bridge's console and on the page at the same time, and the
page label switches to "live from the board".

To do it again for the actual demo, just re-run the nios2-download line. Leave
the bridge up. Add --reset only when you want the page cleared first.

If nios2-terminal needs arguments on your machine:

    python bridge.py --token <TOKEN> --cmd "nios2-terminal -i 0"


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT THIS ACTUALLY IS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_baremetal.c is Karpathy's llama2.c with the operating system removed. Every
neural-network function is byte-for-byte upstream -- only file I/O and memory
allocation changed, because the board has no filesystem and no heap.

Verified on macOS before you got it: identical output to upstream run.c.
The md5 of that OUTPUT is 8e6e99ed83fc476e1a33bc0940ecffa1, and
expected_output.txt is that text.

Model is stories260K: 292K parameters, 1,056,540 bytes, 259,328 multiply-adds
per token. It uses 2.6% of the board's 64 MB SDRAM including working space.

Repo: https://github.com/wilsonwu-ai/vibe-silicon
Page: https://vibe-silicon.wilson-af8.workers.dev


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
APPENDIX - the old objcopy route, and why we stopped using it
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

You can still link the raw .bin files instead of the headers:

    python ..\..\tools\embed_model.py        # downloads both .bin into models\
    copy ..\..\models\*.bin .
    nios2-elf-objcopy -I binary -O elf32-littlenios2 -B nios2 stories260K.bin model.o
    nios2-elf-objcopy -I binary -O elf32-littlenios2 -B nios2 tok512.bin     tok.o
    nios2-elf-gcc -O2 -DBLOBS_FROM_OBJCOPY -mcustom-fpu-cfg=60-2 \
        run_baremetal.c model.o tok.o -o llama.elf -lm

Two traps, both avoided entirely by Step 4:

  1. objcopy builds the symbol name out of the PATH you hand it. Pass
     "models\stories260K.bin" and the symbol becomes
     _binary_models_stories260K_bin_start, which will not link. It must be a
     bare filename, from inside the folder.

  2. objcopy makes no alignment promise, and the code casts the model blob to
     float*. Nios II masks the low bits of an unaligned word load rather than
     trapping, so a misaligned blob produces a wrong story instead of a crash --
     the hardest failure of the day to diagnose. The .h arrays are declared
     __attribute__((aligned(8))), so this cannot happen on the Step 4 path.
     (--set-section-alignment would fix it, but it needs binutils 2.31+ and
     18.1's Nios II binutils is older.)

Use this only if the headers are somehow unavailable.
